stages.title: Early human history and migration
stages.hook: Scientists say that all people alive today share ancestors from Africa. How could people end up living on every continent?
explain: Our species, Homo sapiens, first appeared in Africa. Fossils from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco are about 300,000 years old and are among the oldest known. For a long time people lived by hunting animals and gathering plants.

Over many thousands of years, groups moved out of Africa and spread across Asia, Europe, Australia and the Americas. They walked, followed food and, in some cases, crossed water in boats. People reached Australia at least 50,000 years ago, and the Americas more than 15,000 years ago.
We learn about these journeys from bones, tools, cave art and, more recently, DNA. The evidence keeps growing, so dates are sometimes updated.

example.q: Why do scientists think people first came from Africa?
steps: The oldest Homo sapiens fossils have been found in Africa.
Genetic studies show that people in Africa have the most variety in their DNA.
Both clues point to a long history there, and the other groups later moved out.
example.a: Fossils and DNA both point to Africa.

analogies.home: A family that grows may spread to different towns, but all share the same grandparents.
analogies.nature: Seeds blown from one tree can grow into forests far away.
analogies.sea: People reaching Australia needed boats or rafts to cross open water.

stages.mnemonic: Out of Africa, then everywhere: Africa, Asia, Australia, Europe, Americas.
terms: Moving from one place to live in another.
The preserved remains of a living thing from long ago.
A person who finds food by hunting and gathering wild plants.
The code inside living things that is passed from parents to children.

misc.wrong: Early people all stayed in one place.
misc.right: People moved often and spread over the whole world, including across seas.

stages.limits: Documented fact: Homo sapiens fossils in Africa. Scholarly uncertainty: exact dates and routes of migration, which are revised as new finds appear.

questions.why: Food and climate were the main pushes, and curiosity and growth also led groups to new places.

panel.q: Why are DNA and fossils both needed to study early migration?
panel.model: Fossils show where and when people lived, and DNA shows how groups are related. Together they give a fuller, more reliable picture than either alone.
panel.why: Different kinds of evidence check and strengthen one another.

panel.q: A new fossil is found that is older than any known. What should scientists do?

panel.why: Science follows evidence.

o: All humans share the same species and ancestry

panel.why: All living people are Homo sapiens, with a shared long history.

teach.topic: How people spread around the world
teach.model: Our species first appeared in Africa. Over thousands of years, people moved to find food and better places to live. They spread across Asia, Europe, Australia and the Americas, and we learn about it from fossils and DNA.

stages.title: Ancient African civilisations
stages.hook: Africa has some of the oldest cities and kingdoms in the world. What do pyramids in Egypt and in Sudan have in common?
explain: Ancient Egypt grew along the Nile river. Its farmers used the yearly flood to grow crops. Egyptians built pyramids, such as the Great Pyramid built about 4,500 years ago, and wrote in hieroglyphs.

To the south, in Nubia (today's Sudan), the Kingdom of Kush had its own rulers and built hundreds of pyramids, many at Meroë. Kush once ruled Egypt too, in the period known as the 25th Dynasty. In the highlands of Ethiopia, the Kingdom of Aksum traded by sea and made coins and tall stone stelae.
Other African peoples built their own states. Carthage, in today's Tunisia, was a great trading city. The Nok culture of West Africa made fine clay sculptures and used iron.

example.q: Why was the Nile so important to Egypt?
steps: Most of Egypt is desert.
The Nile flooded each year and left rich soil.
Farmers could grow plenty of food, which supported cities.
example.a: The flood made farmland in a desert land.

analogies.farm: The Nile's flood was like free watering and fertiliser for farms.
analogies.sea: Aksum's ships carried goods across the Red Sea to places far away.
analogies.city: Meroë was a busy city with temples, iron workshops and royal tombs.

stages.mnemonic: Nile, Nubia, Aksum, Carthage: four names for Africa's early powers.
terms: A kingdom in Nubia, in today's Sudan.
A tall carved stone slab or pillar.

misc.wrong: Ancient Egypt was separate from the rest of Africa.
misc.right: Egypt was part of Africa and traded and fought with Nubia and other peoples.

stages.limits: Documented fact: Egyptian pyramids and Kushite pyramids exist. Scholarly uncertainty: details of dates and the Meroitic script, which is not yet fully understood.

stages.title: Ancient Mesopotamia and Persia
stages.hook: The word 'Mesopotamia' means 'between rivers'. Which two rivers do you think it means?
explain: Mesopotamia lies between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, in today's Iraq. The Sumerians built some of the first cities here, such as Uruk, about 5,000 years ago. They invented cuneiform, wedge-shaped writing pressed into clay.
Later, Babylon became powerful. King Hammurabi, who ruled about 3,800 years ago, had a set of laws carved on a stone. Assyria also built a big empire in the same region.
In Iran, the Persian Empire grew. Cyrus the Great founded it around 550 BCE. It was very large and used roads, such as the Royal Road, to send messages.

example.q: Why was writing on clay useful to the Sumerians?
steps: Clay was easy to find by the rivers.
Marks pressed into wet clay dried hard.
The records, such as trade lists, lasted thousands of years.
example.a: Clay was easy to find and made lasting records.

analogies.farm: Canals brought river water to fields, like pipes to a garden.
analogies.city: A Mesopotamian city had temples, markets and a ruler, like a small country.
analogies.tech: Clay tablets were like early hard drives for keeping records.

stages.mnemonic: Tigris and Euphrates: two rivers, many firsts.
terms: The land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers.
Many lands ruled by one government.

misc.wrong: Writing was invented only once and spread everywhere.
misc.right: Writing was invented in several places on its own, such as Mesopotamia, Egypt, China and Mesoamerica.

stages.limits: Documented fact: cuneiform tablets and Hammurabi's stone. Scholarly uncertainty: exact dates and how fairly the laws were used.

stages.title: Ancient Indian civilisations
stages.hook: Some cities 4,500 years ago had drains and straight streets. Who built them?
explain: The Indus Valley civilisation grew along the Indus river in today's Pakistan and northwest India. Its great cities, Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, had straight streets, brick houses and drains. Its mature period was roughly 2600 to 1900 BCE.
The Indus people made seals with a script that nobody has yet been able to read. They traded with Mesopotamia.

Later, in the Ganges region, kingdoms grew. The Maurya Empire was founded by Chandragupta Maurya, and his grandson Ashoka ruled from about 268 BCE. After a war, Ashoka supported Buddhism and carved messages about kindness on pillars and rocks.

example.q: What does a city drain tell us about a society?
steps: Drains need planning.
They show care for cleanliness.
So the society could organise public works.
example.a: It had organised planning for public health.

analogies.city: Planned streets in a modern city echo Harappa's grid.
analogies.home: A bathroom with a drain is like those in Indus houses.
analogies.music: A script with no key is like a song with notes we can see but cannot play.

stages.title: Ancient China and East Asia
stages.hook: Paper, silk and the compass were all first used in China. How might they have changed life?
explain: Ancient China grew along the Yellow River and the Yangtze. The Shang dynasty used oracle bones, the oldest known Chinese writing. Later the Zhou period saw thinkers such as Confucius (551 to 479 BCE), who taught about respect and good government.

In 221 BCE, Qin Shi Huang joined the warring states into one empire. After the Qin, the Han dynasty ruled for four centuries. Under the Han, the Silk Road linked China to Central Asia and beyond, and paper was developed.
Nearby, early Korean and Japanese societies grew too. Rice farming spread across East Asia.

example.q: Why did the Silk Road matter to China and to other lands?
steps: Chinese silk was in demand far away.
Traders carried silk west and brought back horses and goods.
Ideas and religions also travelled the same way.
example.a: It linked distant lands through trade and ideas.

analogies.home: Confucius taught rules of respect for society, as parents teach good manners at home.
analogies.city: The Great Wall and roads were like a big project joined by planning.
analogies.sea: Rivers carried boats as roads of water.

stages.title: Ancient Greece and Rome
stages.hook: Athenians voted in a public assembly 2,500 years ago. Who could vote, and who could not?
explain: Ancient Greece was made of many city-states, such as Athens and Sparta. Around 508 BCE, Athens began a form of democracy. Male citizens could vote in the assembly. Women, enslaved people and foreigners could not. The Greeks also made great works of drama, philosophy and mathematics.

Rome began as a city in Italy. It was a republic, then an empire after Augustus became the first emperor in 27 BCE. At its height, Rome ruled lands around the Mediterranean in Europe, Africa and Asia. It built roads, aqueducts and law. The western Roman Empire ended in 476 CE.
Both Greece and Rome learned from other peoples, including Egyptians, Phoenicians and Persians, and both depended on enslaved labour.

example.q: Why can Athenian democracy be called limited?
steps: Only free adult male citizens voted.
Women, enslaved people and foreigners were excluded.

stages.title: Early American civilisations
stages.hook: Maize, potatoes and chocolate all come from the Americas. Which early peoples grew them?
explain: In Peru, the city of Caral was built about 4,600 years ago, and belongs to the Norte Chico civilisation, one of the oldest in the Americas. In Mexico, the Olmec made huge carved stone heads, from about 1200 BCE.

The Maya lived in southern Mexico and Central America. They built stone cities such as Tikal and Palenque, developed a writing system, and used a calendar and the idea of zero. Their cities flourished especially from about 250 to 900 CE, and Maya people live in the same region today.
In the Andes, Chavín and later peoples farmed on terraces and grew potatoes. Teotihuacan, near today's Mexico City, was one of the biggest cities in the world in its time.

example.q: What do big stone heads tell us about the Olmec?
steps: Carving and moving huge stones took many workers.
So the Olmec had leaders who could organise people.
The heads probably show rulers.
example.a: They had organised leadership and skilled carvers.

analogies.farm: Terraces on hillsides make flat steps for crops.
analogies.city: Tikal had temples and plazas like a city centre.
analogies.music: The Maya calendar had cycles like repeating rhythms.

stages.title: Aboriginal Australian and Pacific histories
stages.hook: Aboriginal peoples have lived in Australia for tens of thousands of years. How have they kept their histories alive?
explain: Aboriginal peoples have lived in Australia for at least 50,000 years, and many scholars think longer, possibly about 65,000 years. Torres Strait Islander peoples, of the islands between Australia and Papua New Guinea, have their own cultures and histories. Both hold histories through oral traditions, songs, art and ceremonies, often called the Dreaming in some Aboriginal traditions. Some stories seem to describe events from long ago, such as rising seas, which is debated by scholars.

Across the Pacific, the Lapita people sailed from island to island about 3,000 years ago. Later, Polynesian navigators settled places such as Hawaii, Rapa Nui and Aotearoa (New Zealand), using knowledge of stars, swells, winds and birds.
Aboriginal peoples also looked after land with care, including fire management, and had many languages.

example.q: How can a navigator find an island without instruments?
steps: Watch the stars rise and set to know direction.
Feel the swells made by far-away land.
Notice birds that fly out to fish and return to land.
example.a: By reading stars, swells and birds.

analogies.home: A grandparent's song can carry a map in its words.

misc.right: Oral traditions are carefully kept and passed on, and can hold true detail for a very long time.

stages.limits: Documented fact: archaeological sites and ongoing cultural knowledge. Oral tradition: Dreaming stories. Scholarly uncertainty: exact date of first arrival in Australia.

stages.title: Foundations of Antarctica's documented exploration history
stages.hook: Nobody has ever lived in Antarctica for generations. So where does its history come from?
explain: Antarctica has no Indigenous population, so its documented history begins with explorers and scientists. Long ago, thinkers in Greece reasoned there must be a southern land to balance the north. The word Antarctic means opposite the Arctic.
In 1773, the British captain James Cook crossed the Antarctic Circle with his ships, the first known to do so. He never saw the continent, but he found the ice too thick to go further.
The first sightings of the continent came in 1820, when ships from Russia, Britain and the United States saw it. Who saw it first is still debated. Early visitors were seal hunters and sailors.

example.q: Why is Cook's voyage important even though he did not see the continent?
steps: He sailed all the way round the south of the world.
He showed any southern land must be small and icy.
So the idea of a rich southern continent faded.
example.a: It showed a great warm southern land was unlikely.

analogies.sea: Ships pushed through cold seas full of floating ice.
analogies.nature: Ice sheets are like huge frozen rivers.
analogies.tech: Explorers used compasses and logs; today scientists use satellites.
